default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_GameProfileExplaine: Performance settings (like refresh rate, framerate limit, etc) can be adjusted for the system as a whole, or on a per-game basis.\n\nIf a title doesn’t have a game-specific performance profile (or this is toggled off), the default system settings will be used.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_AppRefreshRate_Expl:
Specify the maximum frames per second (FPS) the game is allowed to render. Users typically prefer framerate limits near (or slightly lower than) the game's average framerate.

Higher framerates typically produce smoother / lower-latency gameplay, at the expense of increased power usage.

Some games may have adverse effects when refresh rate limiting is enabled, including increased input lag or audio glitches. For these cases it is recommended to set the framerate limit to maximum.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_AppRefreshRate_Rest: A firmware update is required to use this feature.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_DisableFrameLimit_E:
Disabling the frame limit allows games to render as fast as hardware performance allows (potentially higher than the display refresh rate).

This setting may minimize frame latency for some games, but can potentially consume large amounts of power to render frames that will not reach the screen.

It is recommend to keep this setting disabled under normal usage to preserve battery life.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_GamescopeRefreshRat:
Specify the maximum refresh rate for the screen. Users typically prefer refresh rates near (or slightly lower than) the game's average framerate.

Higher refresh rates typically produce smoother / lower-latency gameplay by allowing the game to render at a higher framerate. However, a higher framerate will result in increased power usage.

Some games may have adverse effects when refresh rate switching is enabled, including increased input lag or audio glitches. For these cases it is recommended to set the refresh rate to the maximum allowed value.

default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_Overlay_Explainer: Adjust this setting to control how much data is shown in the performance overlay.\n\nThe performance overlay provides realtime data about the current status of your device, including frames per second, power consumption, GPU and CPU usage and more. This data can be useful to determine how a settings change impacts performance and battery life.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_LimitFrameRate_Expl:
Change this value limit the maximum number of frames per second a game is allowed to render (framerate).

Setting a framerate limit can be useful to stabilize a game's framerate. When a game quickly oscillates between framerates it can make gameplay feel choppy. In this case using a framerate limit that is low enough to produce a non-oscillating framerate can produce a more enjoyable gameplay experience.

Limiting the framerate can also be useful to reduce power consumption.

Some games can have adverse interactions when a framerate limit is enabled, including increased input lag and audio glitches. For these cases it may be desireable to disable the framerate limit.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_FrameLimit_Explaine:
Adjust this setting to limit the maximum number of frames per second a game is allowed to render (framerate). This will automatically set the display’s refresh rate to a multiple of the framerate.

Limiting framerate can be useful for reducing power consumption, as lower framerates require less power. It’s also useful in cases where a game’s framerate is unstable and choppy. Using a limit that’s low enough to stabilize framerate can make for a more enjoyable gameplay experience.

Some games may exhibit issues when a framerate limit is enabled, including increased input lag and audio glitches. In these cases it’s probably better to disable the framerate limit.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_TDPLimit_Explainer_: Adjust this value to limit the maximum amount of power %1$s is allowed to consume.\n\nLowering the TDP limit reduces the amount of work the system is allowed to do per second. This results in improved battery life, but will also reduce the system’s performance while playing games.

Adjust this value to limit the maximum amount of power this device is allowed to consume.\n\nLowering the TDP limit reduces the amount of work the system is allowed to do per second. This results in improved battery life, but will also reduce the system’s performance while playing games.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_GPUClockManual_Expl: Adjust this value to set a fixed clock for the system’s GPU, which can be useful for stabilizing a game’s framerate.\n\nNormally the GPU automatically adjusts clock frequency to balance battery consumption and performance. Some games have drastic transitions between low and high GPU usage, which sometimes hitch if the GPU does not ramp up the clocks fast enough. For these cases it can be useful to set a fixed clock to avoid a hitch due to an underclocked GPU.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_RefreshRate_Explain:
Change this value to set the display's refresh rate.

Adjusting the display's refresh rate can be useful to stabilize a game's framerate. When a game quickly oscillates between framerates it can make gameplay feel choppy. In this lowering the refresh rate to a value that is low enough to produce a non-oscillating framerate can lead to a more enjoyable gameplay experience.

Limiting the framerate can also be useful to reduce power consumption.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_EnableTearing_Expla:
This toggle allows a game to render at a different refresh rate than the display.

Synchronizing the game's render output with the display can introduce latency to the render pipeline. Enabling this setting can mitigate this latency, but can result in tearing artifacts during gameplay.

To take advantage of this setting, VSync must be disabled in the game's settings and the frame limit setting must be turned off.
default.QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_VariableResolution_: Turning on half rate shading forcibly reduces the shading quality used by a game.\n\nThis can improve battery life and performance by reducing the amount of work a game needs to do to generate a new frame. This results in reduced visual quality for games.

default.Developer_SLS_Enabled_Description: Help improve SteamOS by sharing crash reports.
default.Developer_SLS_Enabled_Explainer:
Help improve SteamOS by sharing crash reports with the SteamOS development team.

This information will be used to help improve the reliability and compatibility of SteamOS.

You can configure the categories of data that will be shared. For more details on what data is included in each category please refer to the individual category toggles.
default.Developer_SLS_Minidump_Enabled_Explainer: This report will be generated when an application crashes. This data will be used to help improve application compatibility and reliability with SteamOS.\n\nThe report contains a minidump of the crash with process heap collection disabled. The minidump will contain the runtime stack for each thread at the time of the crash, thread contexts including CPU register values, metadata about the CPU architecture and the executable name and path.
default.Developer_SLS_Kdump_Enabled_Explainer: This report will be generated when the kernel encounters a fatal error. This data will be used to help improve general system stability for SteamOS.\n\nThe report contains a memory dump of the kernel when the crash happened and the kernel logs.
default.Developer_SLS_GPU_Enabled_Explainer: This report will be generated when the system's GPU encounters a fatal error.\n\nThe report includes information reported by the GPU driver regarding the state of the graphics hardware when the error occurred. This may include information about the offending GPU command that caused the crash (if it could be identified), and the application that submitted said command.
default.Developer_SLS_Journal_Enabled_Explainer: Share logs from critical system processes alongside a crash report. This supplementary information can provide the necessary context to help identify and resolve the root cause of a crash.\n\nThis report includes logs for the system update services, the boot management services, steamos management services, the settings management service and the steam crash collection service.
default.Developer_SLS_SystemInfo_Enabled_Explain: This report contains information about the system state. This supplementary information can provide the necessary context to help identify bugs that only happen on certain hardware configurations.\n\nThis report includes RAM and VRAM size, SteamOS branch, hardware revision information, BIOS information, developer mode status, connected USB peripheral details (VID/PID/Manufacturer ID), external display information, connected audio device information, a list of connected bluetooth devices, filesystem and partition layout information, battery health and network interface details (excluding MAC and IP address details).
default.Developer_SLS_Devcoredump_Enabled_Explai: This report will be generated when a driver encounters an unrecoverable error.\n\nThe report includes information reported by the kernel and driver regarding the state of the system when the error occurred. This may include detailed information from the driver that crashed, kernel logs, kernel stack traces and memory information.

To allow you to play any game, even if it doesn't support game controllers, your Deck uses <2>Steam Input</2>, a system that translates your physical inputs into commands for the game.

Controller configuration for your <1></1> uses <2>Steam Input</2>, a system that translates your physical inputs into commands for the game. This allows you to play any game, even if it wasn't designed for your particular controller or doesn't support gamepads.
<1>Commands</1> can be any kind of input that games use - a B button on a gamepad, the Enter key, a left mouse button click, and so on.
Each game's Controller Layout contains a list of all the physical parts of your controller, and what commands are assigned to them.
Customizing is as simple as selecting a physical input, and your desired command.
Deck Verified games always have fully working Controller Layouts, so you can just fire them up and start playing.
By default, they may not use the extra physical inputs the Deck has over standard gamepads, but the <1>Quick Settings</1> section makes it easy to assign commands for those.

default.ControllerConfigurator_Interstitial_Intr: This game has native support for <1>Steam Input</1>, the system Steam uses to translate your physical inputs. With native support, your layout will show Game Actions instead of generic commands.
These games will often contain <1>Action Sets</1> - different control schemes that are used during different parts of the game.
This means you'll be able to fully customize every part of the game to suit your preferences, but only if you choose to. The default layout provided by the game's developer will just work.

Many games have different control schemes for different parts of the game. You might have one control scheme for walking around on foot, another for driving a vehicle, and yet another when viewing a fullscreen map of the game world.

Games that support controllers will usually handle switching between these control schemes for you. But if you're playing a game that wasn't built with controllers in mind, or one that doesn't support controller customization to the level you'd like, you can use <1>Action Sets</1> to do it yourself.

Many games utilize unique control schemes during different scenarios within a game. Within Steam Input we call these Action Sets. For games built without controller support in mind, you may create your own custom Action Sets and switch between them in-game.
Changing which set is active is a command you can assign to any physical input.
Action Sets may also be <1>Layers</1>, which are smaller layouts layered over the top of the Action Set, often only changing the way a single physical input is translated.
For example, some games automatically lower your sensitivity when you zoom in to aim a weapon. For games that don't do it, you could use a Layer to reproduce the behavior.

default.ControllerBinding_CurveExponent_joystick: Stick Response Curve
default.ControllerBinding_CustomCurveExponent_jo: Changing this slider adjusts the output response curve for the joystick.
default.ControllerBinding_CurveExponent_joystick: This determines the mapping of analog input to output.  By default a linear 1:1 mapping is used.  This curve can altered so there is more or less room for fine controls.
Response Curve - Linear
A Linear response curve maps the input directly to the output in a 1:1 fashion.  At 50% deflection, 50% output will be sent.
Response Curve - Aggressive
An aggressive response curve gets to 100% output faster.  This gives less of a slow range and more quickly hits the upper range of output, with faster response.
Response Curve - Relaxed
A relaxed response curve gets to 100% output slower.  There is slightly more slow range where fine control can be used and the upper range is pushed further towards the edges.
Response Curve - Wide

A wide response curve gets to 100% output much slower than default.  There is a wide range of low values which ramps up quickly at the outer edges.  This allows for a wide amount of small values in the inner range while ramping to full at the outside.
Response Curve - Extra Wide
An extra wide response curve provides a large range of lower values over a wide band, only reaching 100% at the extremes.
Response Curve - Custom Curve
A Custom Curve can be defined using the response curve slider.
default.ControllerBinding_AccelerationStyle_Joys: Apply the response curve Per Axis, or based on the Distance from the Deadzone.
The response curve is applied separately to each axis. Moving the stick in a circle will bias movement toward the axes.
The response curve is applied using the distance of the stick from the deadzone. Moving the stick in a circle will have no directional bias.
default.ControllerBinding_AccelerationStyle_Gyro: Apply the response curve Per Axis, or based on the Distance from the Deadzone.
The response curve is applied separately to each axis. The stick output will be biased toward the axes.
The response curve is applied using the distance of the stick from the deadzone. The stick output will have no directional bias.
default.ControllerBinding_DeadZoneInnerRadius_jo: Joystick events won't be sent if within this deadzone.  The slider is a radius of the deadzone, with fully to the left as no deadzone and fully right as the entire radius being deadzone.  Full analog output values are mapped to the zone between the inner and outer deadzone.  Extending out the inner deadzone will allow more area in the deadzone shape where no input is sent.
default.ControllerBinding_DeadZoneOuterRadius_jo: Joystick events will reach maximum upon hitting the outer deadzone.  The slider can be visualized as extending a radius from the center outward.  Full analog output values are mapped to the zone between the inner and outer deadzone.  Pulling in the outer deadzone will cause output to reach its full amount faster.
default.ControllerBinding_DeadZoneShape_joystick: Deadzones can take on different shapes to better match gameplay.  For example, a cross shaped deadzone is often best for movement where holding primarily forward has the side movement within the deadzone so movement doesn't drift for a less than 100% perfect alignment.

The cross shaped deadzone treats each axis separately with the inner deadzone being a band along that axis.  This creates a + shaped cross of deadzone along the axis.  This is often best for navigation where holding primarily in a single direction won't cause drift for a less that 100% perfect alignment.

A simple circle shaped deadzone.  Input in between the inner and outer deadzones is mapped to its relative distance between the two.  Any input inside the inner deadzone is not sent, while outside the outer is fully on in that direction.

The square deadzone uses a cross for determining the inner deadzone, but also maps the output from a circle into a square.  This makes output in the diagonals approach their maximum value more quickly.
default.ControllerBinding_AntiDeadZone_joystick_: Most games apply their own deadzones to controller output. This subtracts away the deadzone, and provides finer grain control within the remaining section.  The higher the slider, the more is added to the smallest output value.  Note that if all deadzone is removed entirely, all positions will cause input. You can use Anti-DeadZone Buffer to allow for a small area where no input will be sent, even if the anti-deadzone is larger than the deadzone of the game.
default.ControllerBinding_AntiDeadZoneBuffer_joy: If an anti-deadzone has been applied, there may be no remaining actual deadzone as applied by the game, so touching anywhere will actively cause movement. default.ControllerBinding_CurveExponentCameraMod: This determines the mapping of analog input to output.  By default a linear 1:1 mapping is used.  This curve can altered so there is more or less room for fine controls.
A Linear response curve maps the input directly to the output in a 1:1 fashion.  At 50% deflection, 50% output will be sent.
An aggressive response curve gets to 100% output faster.  This gives less of a slow range and more quickly hits the upper range of output, with faster response.
A relaxed response curve gets to 100% output slower.  There is slightly more slow range where fine control can be used and the upper range is pushed further towards the edges.

A wide response curve gets to 100% output much slower that default.  There is a wide range of low values which ramps up quickly at the outer edges.  This allows for a wide amount of small values in the inner range while ramping to full at the outside.
An extra wide response curve provides a large range of lower values over a wide band, only reaching 100% at the extremes.

default.ControllerBinding_TriggerClick_Descripti: This command will be performed when you pull the trigger the entire way until it clicks (you'll hear a soft click).
default.ControllerBinding_HoldRepeatsTrigger_On_: If turned on, holding any button will cause it to repeat.  This is often known as a 'Turbo Mode'.
default.ControllerBinding_HoldRepeatsTrigger_Off: If turned on, holding any button will cause it to repeat.  This is often known as a 'Turbo Mode'.
default.ControllerBinding_HoldRepeatIntervalTrig: When Turbo Mode is turned on, this determines the speed of the repeat.  Slide to the right for a faster repeat rate.
default.ControllerBinding_OutputTrigger_Descript: When enabled, the analog value of the specified trigger will be sent to the game.  Only possible if the game recognizes XInput compatible gamepad values.
default.ControllerBinding_OutputTrigger_TriggerO: No analog values will be sent.
default.ControllerBinding_OutputTrigger_TriggerL: Analog values will be sent to the game as a Left Trigger.  Only possible if the game recognizes XInput compatible gamepad values.
default.ControllerBinding_OutputTrigger_TriggerR: Analog values will be sent to the game as a Right Trigger.  Only possible if the game recognizes XInput compatible gamepad values.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerDeadZoneStart_D: This sets the deadzone for the analog trigger.  A greater value will create more of a 'deadzone' where no analog value will be sent when initially pressing the trigger down.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerDeadZoneEnd_Des: This sets the deadzone for the analog trigger.  A smaller value will create more of a 'deadzone' at the end of the range where the maximum analog value will be sent once past this point in the throw.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_D: This determines the mapping of analog input to output.  By default a linear 1:1 mapping is used.  This curve can altered so there is more or less room for fine controls.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_L: A Linear response curve maps the input directly to the output in a 1:1 fashion.  At 50% deflection, 50% output will be sent.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_1: An aggressive response curve gets to 100% output faster.  This gives less of a slow range and more quickly hits the upper range of output, with faster response.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_2: A relaxed response curve gets to 100% output slower.  There is slightly more slow range where fine control can be used and the upper range is pushed further towards the end.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_3: A wide response curve gets to 100% output much slower that default.  There is a wide range of low values which ramps up quickly at the end.  This allows for a wide amount of small values in the inner range while ramping to full at the outside.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_4: An extra wide response curve provides a large range of lower values over a wide band, only reaching 100% at the extremes.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_C: A Custom Curve can be defined using the response curve slider.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerCustomCurveExpo: Changing this slider adjusts the output response curve for the trigger.
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerAnalogThreshold: This command will be performed when you pull the trigger softly, but not the entire way (so you won't hear the full pull click).
default.ControllerBinding_TriggerThreshold_Descr: The Soft Pull command will be sent when the trigger is pulled past this point.  For a light press, move the slider to the left, while one requiring a farther press of the trigger should be moved to the right.
default.ControllerBinding_AdaptiveThreshold_Desc: In a game where dual stage triggers are enabled via the threshold as well as the click, hip fire allows a quick pull of the trigger to hit the physical button without engaging the threshold command, while a slower pull will engage the threshold first.  Aggressive Hip Fire will engage the threshold command much faster than Relaxed.
default.ControllerBinding_AdaptiveThreshold_Trig: Good for mouse clicks and drags. As the trigger is pulled, the Soft Pull command is sent first, followed by the Full Pull.
Good for action games where you want to be able to rapidly send the Soft Pull command with quick pulls & releases.
Good for action games with both Full Pull and Soft Pull commands assigned. Quick pulls will only send the Full Pull, whereas slower pulls will send the Soft Pull first, followed by the Full Pull.
Same as the above, but with a larger time window in which the Soft Pull can be skipped.
An even larger time window in which the Soft Pull can be skipped.
Like the above options, except that once either of the Full Pull or Soft Pull commands have been sent, the other cannot be sent until the trigger has been fully released.
default.ControllerBinding_AdaptiveThreshold_Hair: With the Hair Trigger setting, the threshold will adapt to the user.  Once the initial threshold has been passed, letting off the trigger by any degree will reset the trigger, allowing it to be pressed again, even if the trigger hasn't been released to the point of the initial threshold.  This is often desirable for situations like rapid firing a weapon where you want a small amount of throw to fire the first shot, but you don't want to have to let it return to full unpressed to fire again.  For commands that require holding the trigger continually, it may be less desirable, as any lessing of the trigger will cause the selected command to release.
default.ControllerBinding_AdaptiveThreshold_Simp: Basic Threshold, the threshold is at a fixed throw specified by the selected value.  Once the specified threshold has been passed, letting off the trigger will not release the button until the trigger has been released to the point of the specified threshold.  For commands that require holding the trigger continually, where accidental button release is undesirable, this may be the preferred setting.
default.ControllerBinding_AdaptiveThreshold_Long: Intended to be used with a dual-stage trigger setup, Hip Fire allows a quick pull of the trigger to engage the click without engaging the threshold.  A slower pull or hover will engage the threshold command.  This allows for commands such as iron-sights to be set on the threshold and fire on the click, while still allowing a quick pull to click to fire without entering iron-sights.  Additionally, once the click has been hit, the threshold won't be engaged until the trigger has been released outside of the threshold range, allowing it to be primed for additional clicks.  Aggressive Hip Fire mode is a very small window before engaging the threshold, requiring a very fast pull of the trigger to skip it.  The Threshold command will engage fastest here when intentionally enaging it.

Intended to be used with a dual-stage trigger setup, Hip Fire allows a quick pull of the trigger to engage the click without engaging the threshold.  A slower pull or hover will engage the threshold command.  This allows for commands such as iron-sights to be set on the threshold and fire on the click, while still allowing a quick pull to click to fire without entering iron-sights.  Additionally, once the click has been hit, the threshold won't be engaged until the trigger has been released outside of the threshold range, allowing it to be primed for additional clicks.  Normal Hip Fire mode has a window before engaging the threshold, requiring a quick pull of the trigger to avoid it.

PartnerEvent_MM_TitleTip: Make the title compelling and relevant for players. If this is truly one of the biggest updates of the year, the title should reflect that excitement. Avoid generic phrasing like <1>'Version 330.4 update.'</1> Instead, highlight what makes the update special.
PartnerEvent_MM_ArtworkTip: The key art must clearly showcase the update itself. Do not simply reuse your game's standard artwork. Players should immediately recognize that this represents something new and significant.
PartnerEvent_MM_DescriptionTip1: The event description should be thoughtfully built to explain the update and why it matters. Use this as your chance to bring players back into your game:
PartnerEvent_MM_DescriptionTip2: Highlight the new and exciting content.
PartnerEvent_MM_DescriptionTip3: Get creative with images, trailers, or short clips.

promo_steamawards2020_cat50_desc: Maybe it was its immersive gameplay, or its gripping story... its well-crafted characters, immaculate design, or addictive multiplayer. Whatever the reason, the winner of 2020's Game of the Year Award is an instant classic.
promo_steamawards2020_cat51_desc: The VR Game of the Year isn't merely masquerading as regular reality. This game improves on reality, taking advantage of the medium of VR and pushing the boundaries of the virtual realm.
promo_steamawards2020_cat52_desc: This game has been out for a while. The team is well past the debut of their creative baby, but being the good parents they are, these devs continue to nurture and support their creation. This game, to this day, is still getting new content after all these years.
promo_steamawards2020_cat53_desc: There are some games out there that just aren't the same when you play by yourself. Maybe you need to have a friend to watch your back. Maybe you need to have a friend that you can stab in their back. Either way, fun is awaiting those who gather friends together play this game.
promo_steamawards2020_cat54_desc: Visual style doesn't aspire to real-world graphical fidelity (though a noble goal in itself)… it describes a distinctive look and feel that suffuses an entire game.
promo_steamawards2020_cat55_desc: The designers of this game are at the front lines of creative experimentation, bringing a fresh perspective and brain-breaking surprises. This game delighted, inspired and entertained with newness never played before.
promo_steamawards2020_cat56_desc: This is the game that rewards persistence, and is not for the faint of heart. It's the toughest game we've ever loved.
promo_steamawards2020_cat57_desc: This unsung hero deserves to be recognized for its outstanding musical score. It's the OST with the MOST!
promo_steamawards2020_cat58_desc: Some days, only a narrative-heavy game will hit the spot, and this one packs a wallop. It's as gripping as any soap opera, and as well-tuned as a prestige-TV screenplay. Bravissimo -- for making us feel things!
promo_steamawards2020_cat59_desc: This game is the antidote to a busy day. It's smooth, it's relaxing, it lets your worries melt away. This game is your moment of zen.

Lunar2020_StoryDayOne:
The Jade Emperor summoned all creatures of his kingdom to race to the heavenly palace, declaring the first twelve to arrive would be honored with a place on his new calendar.

Clever Rat was the first to cross the river into the celestial domain. No fan of swimming, Rat hitched a ride atop the trusty Ox—excitedly jumping into the Emperor's garden just before the pair were set to reach shore.

Steady Ox crossed the river with ease. Unconcerned with the results of the race, Ox felt content with a role in Rat's success.
Lunar2020_StoryDayTwo:
Self-sufficient Tiger traveled too carefully to outpace Ox, thinking it better to arrive third than not at all.

Swift Rabbit hopped a log floating nowhere fast. But luck paid off where strategy didn't, and a helpful wind sped the makeshift boat safely on its way.

Flying Dragon's vantage revealed a village in need, so of course Dragon stopped to help—even gifting Rabbit a gust across the river. Honor was far more important than victory, and Dragon found fifth place a fine fit.
Lunar2020_StoryDayThree: Stealthy Snake had little interest in a long-distance effort, so it wrapped itself unnoticed around Horse's front hoof.\n\nAs Horse galloped towards the finish line, Snake uncoiled, startling the steed just long enough to slither into sixth—with the skittish Horse trotting close behind.
Lunar2020_StoryDayFour:
Goat, Monkey, and Rooster worked together, but let Goat claim eighth as the backbone of their journey. Cheerful Monkey was next, and the strutting Rooster crossed tenth, proud that the order was fair.

Playful Dog was mostly interested in splashing around, feeling eleventh a fine trade for all the fun.

Last came Pig, who'd stopped for a snack n' a snooze—wise enough to know that each animal will have their time in the Emperor's favor.

QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_GameProfileExplaine: Performance settings (like refresh rate, framerate limit, etc) can be adjusted for the system as a whole, or on a per-game basis.\n\nIf a title doesn’t have a game-specific performance profile (or this is toggled off), the default system settings will be used.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_AppRefreshRate_Expl:
Specify the maximum frames per second (FPS) the game is allowed to render. Users typically prefer framerate limits near (or slightly lower than) the game's average framerate.

Higher framerates typically produce smoother / lower-latency gameplay, at the expense of increased power usage.

Some games may have adverse effects when refresh rate limiting is enabled, including increased input lag or audio glitches. For these cases it is recommended to set the framerate limit to maximum.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_AppRefreshRate_Rest: A firmware update is required to use this feature.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_DisableFrameLimit_E:
Disabling the frame limit allows games to render as fast as hardware performance allows (potentially higher than the display refresh rate).

This setting may minimize frame latency for some games, but can potentially consume large amounts of power to render frames that will not reach the screen.

It is recommend to keep this setting disabled under normal usage to preserve battery life.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_GamescopeRefreshRat:
Specify the maximum refresh rate for the screen. Users typically prefer refresh rates near (or slightly lower than) the game's average framerate.

Higher refresh rates typically produce smoother / lower-latency gameplay by allowing the game to render at a higher framerate. However, a higher framerate will result in increased power usage.

Some games may have adverse effects when refresh rate switching is enabled, including increased input lag or audio glitches. For these cases it is recommended to set the refresh rate to the maximum allowed value.

QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_Overlay_Explainer: Adjust this setting to control how much data is shown in the performance overlay.\n\nThe performance overlay provides realtime data about the current status of your device, including frames per second, power consumption, GPU and CPU usage and more. This data can be useful to determine how a settings change impacts performance and battery life.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_LimitFrameRate_Expl:
Change this value limit the maximum number of frames per second a game is allowed to render (framerate).

Setting a framerate limit can be useful to stabilize a game's framerate. When a game quickly oscillates between framerates it can make gameplay feel choppy. In this case using a framerate limit that is low enough to produce a non-oscillating framerate can produce a more enjoyable gameplay experience.

Limiting the framerate can also be useful to reduce power consumption.

Some games can have adverse interactions when a framerate limit is enabled, including increased input lag and audio glitches. For these cases it may be desireable to disable the framerate limit.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_FrameLimit_Explaine:
Adjust this setting to limit the maximum number of frames per second a game is allowed to render (framerate). This will automatically set the display’s refresh rate to a multiple of the framerate.

Limiting framerate can be useful for reducing power consumption, as lower framerates require less power. It’s also useful in cases where a game’s framerate is unstable and choppy. Using a limit that’s low enough to stabilize framerate can make for a more enjoyable gameplay experience.

Some games may exhibit issues when a framerate limit is enabled, including increased input lag and audio glitches. In these cases it’s probably better to disable the framerate limit.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_TDPLimit_Explainer_: Adjust this value to limit the maximum amount of power %1$s is allowed to consume.\n\nLowering the TDP limit reduces the amount of work the system is allowed to do per second. This results in improved battery life, but will also reduce the system’s performance while playing games.

Adjust this value to limit the maximum amount of power this device is allowed to consume.\n\nLowering the TDP limit reduces the amount of work the system is allowed to do per second. This results in improved battery life, but will also reduce the system’s performance while playing games.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_GPUClockManual_Expl: Adjust this value to set a fixed clock for the system’s GPU, which can be useful for stabilizing a game’s framerate.\n\nNormally the GPU automatically adjusts clock frequency to balance battery consumption and performance. Some games have drastic transitions between low and high GPU usage, which sometimes hitch if the GPU does not ramp up the clocks fast enough. For these cases it can be useful to set a fixed clock to avoid a hitch due to an underclocked GPU.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_RefreshRate_Explain:
Change this value to set the display's refresh rate.

Adjusting the display's refresh rate can be useful to stabilize a game's framerate. When a game quickly oscillates between framerates it can make gameplay feel choppy. In this lowering the refresh rate to a value that is low enough to produce a non-oscillating framerate can lead to a more enjoyable gameplay experience.

Limiting the framerate can also be useful to reduce power consumption.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_EnableTearing_Expla:
This toggle allows a game to render at a different refresh rate than the display.

Synchronizing the game's render output with the display can introduce latency to the render pipeline. Enabling this setting can mitigate this latency, but can result in tearing artifacts during gameplay.

To take advantage of this setting, VSync must be disabled in the game's settings and the frame limit setting must be turned off.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_VariableResolution_: Turning on half rate shading forcibly reduces the shading quality used by a game.\n\nThis can improve battery life and performance by reducing the amount of work a game needs to do to generate a new frame. This results in reduced visual quality for games.
QuickAccess_Tab_Perf_ScalingScaler_Expla: Change this value to modify how windows smaller than the current screen resolution get scaled to fit the screen.

Developer_SLS_Enabled_Description: Help improve SteamOS by sharing crash reports.
Developer_SLS_Enabled_Explainer:
Help improve SteamOS by sharing crash reports with the SteamOS development team.

This information will be used to help improve the reliability and compatibility of SteamOS.

You can configure the categories of data that will be shared. For more details on what data is included in each category please refer to the individual category toggles.
Developer_SLS_Minidump_Enabled_Explainer: This report will be generated when an application crashes. This data will be used to help improve application compatibility and reliability with SteamOS.\n\nThe report contains a minidump of the crash with process heap collection disabled. The minidump will contain the runtime stack for each thread at the time of the crash, thread contexts including CPU register values, metadata about the CPU architecture and the executable name and path.
Developer_SLS_Kdump_Enabled_Explainer: This report will be generated when the kernel encounters a fatal error. This data will be used to help improve general system stability for SteamOS.\n\nThe report contains a memory dump of the kernel when the crash happened and the kernel logs.
Developer_SLS_GPU_Enabled_Explainer: This report will be generated when the system's GPU encounters a fatal error.\n\nThe report includes information reported by the GPU driver regarding the state of the graphics hardware when the error occurred. This may include information about the offending GPU command that caused the crash (if it could be identified), and the application that submitted said command.
Developer_SLS_Journal_Enabled_Explainer: Share logs from critical system processes alongside a crash report. This supplementary information can provide the necessary context to help identify and resolve the root cause of a crash.\n\nThis report includes logs for the system update services, the boot management services, steamos management services, the settings management service and the steam crash collection service.
Developer_SLS_SystemInfo_Enabled_Explain: This report contains information about the system state. This supplementary information can provide the necessary context to help identify bugs that only happen on certain hardware configurations.\n\nThis report includes RAM and VRAM size, SteamOS branch, hardware revision information, BIOS information, developer mode status, connected USB peripheral details (VID/PID/Manufacturer ID), external display information, connected audio device information, a list of connected bluetooth devices, filesystem and partition layout information, battery health and network interface details (excluding MAC and IP address details).
Developer_SLS_Devcoredump_Enabled_Explai: This report will be generated when a driver encounters an unrecoverable error.\n\nThe report includes information reported by the kernel and driver regarding the state of the system when the error occurred. This may include detailed information from the driver that crashed, kernel logs, kernel stack traces and memory information.

ControllerConfigurator_Interstitial_Intr: Steam Input
To allow you to play any game, even if it doesn't support game controllers, your Deck uses <2>Steam Input</2>, a system that translates your physical inputs into commands for the game.

Controller configuration for your <1></1> uses <2>Steam Input</2>, a system that translates your physical inputs into commands for the game. This allows you to play any game, even if it wasn't designed for your particular controller or doesn't support gamepads.
<1>Commands</1> can be any kind of input that games use - a B button on a gamepad, the Enter key, a left mouse button click, and so on.
Each game's Controller Layout contains a list of all the physical parts of your controller, and what commands are assigned to them.
Customizing is as simple as selecting a physical input, and your desired command.
Deck Verified games always have fully working Controller Layouts, so you can just fire them up and start playing.
By default, they may not use the extra physical inputs the Deck has over standard gamepads, but the <1>Quick Settings</1> section makes it easy to assign commands for those.
By default, they may not use the extra physical inputs the Deck has over standard gamepads, but the <1>Quick Settings</1> section makes it easy to assign commands for those.
ControllerConfigurator_Interstitial_NonV: When playing non-verified games from your library, you may need to adjust your controller layout in order to make your game play better with your device’s controls.
Our default templates work for most games, but otherwise we always suggest checking the game's Community Layouts to see if another player has published a custom layout.
These games may ask you to press keys or buttons. In those cases, you’ll need to assign those commands to your device’s physical controls.
Even when the game asks you to press a button that your device has, you will need to assign a matching command.
Even when the game asks you to press a button that the <1></1> has, you will need to assign a matching command.
Even when the game asks you to press a button that the Deck has, your layout may have a different command assigned to that physical button.
Even when the game asks you to press a button that the <1></1> has, your layout may have a different command assigned to that physical button.
It's often a good technique to find the in-game control settings, which will contain a list of all the commands the game expects.
And then assign each of them to one of the Deck's physical inputs.
But remember to always check the Community Layouts first - some other player has probably done this already.
ControllerConfigurator_Interstitial_Gyro: The gyro allows you to move the Deck itself to control a game. This can be very useful for fine control of a first or third person camera.
The gyro allows you to move the gamepad itself to control a game. This can be very useful for fine control of a first or third person camera.

By default, the gyro only sends input to the game when you're touching the <1>Right Joystick</1> or <2>Right Trackpad</2>. It's easy to change this behavior in the gyro settings, but we've found it to work well.
By default, the gyro only sends input to the game when you're touching the <1>Right Trackpad</1>. It's easy to change this behavior in the gyro settings, but we've found it to work well.

By default, the gyro always sends input to the game. It's easy to change this behavior in the gyro settings and depending on the game you might want to use a button to turn off the gyro in order to reposition controller without affecting your aim.

Many games have different control schemes for different parts of the game. You might have one control scheme for walking around on foot, another for driving a vehicle, and yet another when viewing a fullscreen map of the game world.

Games that support controllers will usually handle switching between these control schemes for you. But if you're playing a game that wasn't built with controllers in mind, or one that doesn't support controller customization to the level you'd like, you can use <1>Action Sets</1> to do it yourself.

Many games utilize unique control schemes during different scenarios within a game. Within Steam Input we call these Action Sets. For games built without controller support in mind, you may create your own custom Action Sets and switch between them in-game.
Changing which set is active is a command you can assign to any physical input.
Action Sets may also be <1>Layers</1>, which are smaller layouts layered over the top of the Action Set, often only changing the way a single physical input is translated.
For example, some games automatically lower your sensitivity when you zoom in to aim a weapon. For games that don't do it, you could use a Layer to reproduce the behavior.

ControllerBinding_CurveExponent_joystick: Stick Response Curve
ControllerBinding_CustomCurveExponent_jo: Changing this slider adjusts the output response curve for the joystick.
ControllerBinding_CurveExponent_joystick: This determines the mapping of analog input to output.  By default a linear 1:1 mapping is used.  This curve can altered so there is more or less room for fine controls.
Response Curve - Linear
A Linear response curve maps the input directly to the output in a 1:1 fashion.  At 50% deflection, 50% output will be sent.
Response Curve - Aggressive
An aggressive response curve gets to 100% output faster.  This gives less of a slow range and more quickly hits the upper range of output, with faster response.
Response Curve - Relaxed
A relaxed response curve gets to 100% output slower.  There is slightly more slow range where fine control can be used and the upper range is pushed further towards the edges.
Response Curve - Wide

A wide response curve gets to 100% output much slower than default.  There is a wide range of low values which ramps up quickly at the outer edges.  This allows for a wide amount of small values in the inner range while ramping to full at the outside.
Response Curve - Extra Wide
An extra wide response curve provides a large range of lower values over a wide band, only reaching 100% at the extremes.
Response Curve - Custom Curve
A Custom Curve can be defined using the response curve slider.
ControllerBinding_AccelerationStyle_Joys: Apply the response curve Per Axis, or based on the Distance from the Deadzone.
The response curve is applied separately to each axis. Moving the stick in a circle will bias movement toward the axes.
The response curve is applied using the distance of the stick from the deadzone. Moving the stick in a circle will have no directional bias.
ControllerBinding_AccelerationStyle_Gyro: Apply the response curve Per Axis, or based on the Distance from the Deadzone.

ControllerBinding_DeadZoneInnerRadius_jo: Joystick events won't be sent if within this deadzone.  The slider is a radius of the deadzone, with fully to the left as no deadzone and fully right as the entire radius being deadzone.  Full analog output values are mapped to the zone between the inner and outer deadzone.  Extending out the inner deadzone will allow more area in the deadzone shape where no input is sent.
ControllerBinding_DeadZoneOuterRadius_jo: Joystick events will reach maximum upon hitting the outer deadzone.  The slider can be visualized as extending a radius from the center outward.  Full analog output values are mapped to the zone between the inner and outer deadzone.  Pulling in the outer deadzone will cause output to reach its full amount faster.
ControllerBinding_DeadZoneShape_joystick: Deadzones can take on different shapes to better match gameplay.  For example, a cross shaped deadzone is often best for movement where holding primarily forward has the side movement within the deadzone so movement doesn't drift for a less than 100% perfect alignment.

The cross shaped deadzone treats each axis separately with the inner deadzone being a band along that axis.  This creates a + shaped cross of deadzone along the axis.  This is often best for navigation where holding primarily in a single direction won't cause drift for a less that 100% perfect alignment.

A simple circle shaped deadzone.  Input in between the inner and outer deadzones is mapped to its relative distance between the two.  Any input inside the inner deadzone is not sent, while outside the outer is fully on in that direction.

The square deadzone uses a cross for determining the inner deadzone, but also maps the output from a circle into a square.  This makes output in the diagonals approach their maximum value more quickly.
ControllerBinding_AntiDeadZone_joystick_: Most games apply their own deadzones to controller output. If the control feels 'mushy' with a physical area of movement where no output is seen in game, it is likely caused by the game's deadzone. You can remove this using the Anti-Deadzone setting. This subtracts away the deadzone, and provides finer grain control within the remaining section.  The higher the slider, the more is added to the smallest output value.  Note that if all deadzone is removed entirely, all positions will cause input. You can use Anti-DeadZone Buffer to allow for a small area where no input will be sent, even if the anti-deadzone is larger than the deadzone of the game.
ControllerBinding_AntiDeadZoneBuffer_joy: If an anti-deadzone has been applied, there may be no remaining actual deadzone as applied by the game, so touching anywhere will actively cause movement.  To allow for a safe buffer area where no input will be sent, the anti-deadzone buffer acts as the new deadzone for the control.  It can be visualized as a radius from the center of the pad, within which no input will be sent.

Note that if all deadzone is removed entirely, all positions will cause input. You can use Anti-DeadZone Buffer to allow for a small area where no input will be sent, even if the anti-deadzone is larger than the deadzone of the game.
ControllerBinding_AntiDeadZoneBufferJoys: If an anti-deadzone has been applied, there may be no remaining actual deadzone as applied by the game, so touching anywhere will actively cause movement.  To allow for a safe buffer area where no input will be sent, the anti-deadzone buffer acts as the new deadzone for the control.  It can be visualized as a radius from the center of the pad, within which no input will be sent.

ControllerBinding_VerticalSensitivity_De: Vertical Sensitivity Scale determines how much vertical movement occurs relative to horizontal movement. ControllerBinding_FrictionMouseJoystick_: Trackball friction determines how quickly the trackball slows to a stop when freely spinning.
If off the trackball will have no momentum.  It will act as if trackball mode is disabled.
With Low Friction, the trackball will continue to rotate for a long period after being flicked, slowly coming to a stop.
With Medium Friction, the trackball will rotate for a period after being flicked, gradually coming to a stop.
With High Friction, the trackball will spin for a short duration, quickly come to a stop after being flicked.
With No Friction, the trackball will spin forever after being flicked without outside intervention.
ControllerBinding_VerticalFrictionMouseJ: Vertical Friction determines how fast the vertical movement comes to a stop relative to horizontal movement.  At 50% along the slider it is equal, if less than half it will slow less quickly, if more, more quickly.  For games were you control the camera, it is usually desirable to have high vertical friction so flicks are primarily used for spinning the camera along the horizontal axis.
ControllerBinding_VerticalSensitivityMou: Vertical Sensitivity Scale determines how much vertical movement occurs relative to horizontal movement.  At 50% along the slider it is equal, if less than half it vertical movement will be lower than horizontal, while more will increase the ratio to more vertical movement.
ControllerBinding_SmoothingMouseJoystick: Smoothing helps to remove noise and jitter from the mouse.  Smaller values will result in less filtering, while higher values will be more filtered and smoother.
ControllerBinding_AccelerationMouseJoyst: Acceleration will cause faster movements to cause more mouse movement relative to slow movements for the same space covered on the pad.
With no acceleration movement will be 1:1, with the distance covered on the pad always resulting in the same in-game output regardless of the speed.
With low acceleration movement will be slightly accelerated, with faster movements making in-game output slightly greater at faster speeds for the same distance covered on the physical pad.
With medium acceleration movement will be fairly accelerated, with faster movements making in-game output quite a bit greater at faster speeds for the same distance covered on the physical pad.
With high acceleration movement will be very accelerated, with faster movements making in-game output extremely high at faster speeds for the same distance covered on the physical pad.

ControllerBinding_TriggerClick_Descripti: This command will be performed when you pull the trigger the entire way until it clicks (you'll hear a soft click).
ControllerBinding_HoldRepeatsTrigger_On_: If turned on, holding any button will cause it to repeat.  This is often known as a 'Turbo Mode'.
ControllerBinding_HoldRepeatsTrigger_Off: If turned on, holding any button will cause it to repeat.  This is often known as a 'Turbo Mode'.
ControllerBinding_HoldRepeatIntervalTrig: When Turbo Mode is turned on, this determines the speed of the repeat.  Slide to the right for a faster repeat rate.
ControllerBinding_OutputTrigger_Descript: When enabled, the analog value of the specified trigger will be sent to the game.  Only possible if the game recognizes XInput compatible gamepad values.
ControllerBinding_OutputTrigger_TriggerO: No analog values will be sent.
ControllerBinding_OutputTrigger_TriggerL: Analog values will be sent to the game as a Left Trigger.  Only possible if the game recognizes XInput compatible gamepad values.
ControllerBinding_OutputTrigger_TriggerR: Analog values will be sent to the game as a Right Trigger.  Only possible if the game recognizes XInput compatible gamepad values.
ControllerBinding_TriggerDeadZoneStart_D: This sets the deadzone for the analog trigger.  A greater value will create more of a 'deadzone' where no analog value will be sent when initially pressing the trigger down.
ControllerBinding_TriggerDeadZoneEnd_Des: This sets the deadzone for the analog trigger.  A smaller value will create more of a 'deadzone' at the end of the range where the maximum analog value will be sent once past this point in the throw.
ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_D: This determines the mapping of analog input to output.  By default a linear 1:1 mapping is used.  This curve can altered so there is more or less room for fine controls.
ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_L: A Linear response curve maps the input directly to the output in a 1:1 fashion.  At 50% deflection, 50% output will be sent.
ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_1: An aggressive response curve gets to 100% output faster.  This gives less of a slow range and more quickly hits the upper range of output, with faster response.
ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_2: A relaxed response curve gets to 100% output slower.  There is slightly more slow range where fine control can be used and the upper range is pushed further towards the end.
ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_3: A wide response curve gets to 100% output much slower that default.  There is a wide range of low values which ramps up quickly at the end.  This allows for a wide amount of small values in the inner range while ramping to full at the outside.
ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_4: An extra wide response curve provides a large range of lower values over a wide band, only reaching 100% at the extremes.
ControllerBinding_TriggerCurveExponent_C: A Custom Curve can be defined using the response curve slider.
ControllerBinding_TriggerCustomCurveExpo: Changing this slider adjusts the output response curve for the trigger.
ControllerBinding_TriggerAnalogThreshold: This command will be performed when you pull the trigger softly, but not the entire way (so you won't hear the full pull click).
ControllerBinding_TriggerThreshold_Descr: The Soft Pull command will be sent when the trigger is pulled past this point.  For a light press, move the slider to the left, while one requiring a farther press of the trigger should be moved to the right.
ControllerBinding_AdaptiveThreshold_Desc: In a game where dual stage triggers are enabled via the threshold as well as the click, hip fire allows a quick pull of the trigger to hit the physical button without engaging the threshold command, while a slower pull will engage the threshold first.  Aggressive Hip Fire will engage the threshold command much faster than Relaxed.
ControllerBinding_AdaptiveThreshold_Trig: Good for mouse clicks and drags. As the trigger is pulled, the Soft Pull command is sent first, followed by the Full Pull.
Good for action games where you want to be able to rapidly send the Soft Pull command with quick pulls & releases.
Good for action games with both Full Pull and Soft Pull commands assigned. Quick pulls will only send the Full Pull, whereas slower pulls will send the Soft Pull first, followed by the Full Pull.
Same as the above, but with a larger time window in which the Soft Pull can be skipped.
An even larger time window in which the Soft Pull can be skipped.
Like the above options, except that once either of the Full Pull or Soft Pull commands have been sent, the other cannot be sent until the trigger has been fully released.
ControllerBinding_AdaptiveThreshold_Hair: With the Hair Trigger setting, the threshold will adapt to the user.  Once the initial threshold has been passed, letting off the trigger by any degree will reset the trigger, allowing it to be pressed again, even if the trigger hasn't been released to the point of the initial threshold.  This is often desirable for situations like rapid firing a weapon where you want a small amount of throw to fire the first shot, but you don't want to have to let it return to full unpressed to fire again.  For commands that require holding the trigger continually, it may be less desirable, as any lessing of the trigger will cause the selected command to release.
ControllerBinding_AdaptiveThreshold_Simp: Basic Threshold, the threshold is at a fixed throw specified by the selected value.  Once the specified threshold has been passed, letting off the trigger will not release the button until the trigger has been released to the point of the specified threshold.  For commands that require holding the trigger continually, where accidental button release is undesirable, this may be the preferred setting.
ControllerBinding_AdaptiveThreshold_Long: Intended to be used with a dual-stage trigger setup, Hip Fire allows a quick pull of the trigger to engage the click without engaging the threshold.  A slower pull or hover will engage the threshold command.  This allows for commands such as iron-sights to be set on the threshold and fire on the click, while still allowing a quick pull to click to fire without entering iron-sights.
